pages.x: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a shiny metal ball the size of a beach ball, the first artificial satellite. Its beeping radio signal could be picked up around the world. Americans were shocked that their Cold War rival had beaten them, and might reach them with nuclear missiles too.

A month later Sputnik 2 carried a passenger: Laika, a stray dog from the streets of Moscow. She was the first animal to circle the Earth, but there was no way to bring her back, and she died within hours from the heat. In 1960 two more space dogs, Belka and Strelka, came home safely.

On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin, a 27-year-old Soviet pilot and the son of a carpenter, flew once around the Earth in his Vostok capsule, in 108 minutes. As he lifted off he called out, let's go. He became the most famous man in the world. In 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space.

pages.t: We choose to go to the Moon
pages.x: President John F. Kennedy answered with a promise: Americans would land a man on the Moon and bring him home before the decade was out. In Houston in 1962 he said they would go not because it was easy, but because it was hard. The Apollo programme came to employ some 400,000 people.

In January 1967 a fire swept through the Apollo 1 capsule during a test on the launch pad, killing the astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee. Months later the Soviet cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov died when his capsule's parachute failed.

On 20 July 1969 the lunar module Eagle landed on the Moon's Sea of Tranquillity, and Neil Armstrong stepped down and called it one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind. Buzz Aldrin joined him, while Michael Collins circled overhead. Some 600 million people watched on television.
Rockets and satellites, fuel cells and tiny computers for spacecraft, and the first pictures of the whole Earth from space, like Earthrise, taken from Apollo 8 in 1968.
pages.fx: Satellites now carry phone calls and weather forecasts and tell us where we are, and the pictures of a small blue Earth helped start the movement to protect the environment.

pages.x: Six Apollo crews walked on the Moon until 1972, twelve men in all. In 1975 an American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft docked in orbit, and their commanders shook hands through the hatch. The race was over, and the rivals began to work together in space.

The space race was a contest of the Cold War, fought with rockets built to carry bombs, but it gave humanity its first steps off the Earth. No one has walked on the Moon since 1972, but people have lived in space without a break since 2000, on the International Space Station.
